title: New Mitsubishi Pajero’s Australian Pricing Hints at What U.S. Model Might Cost
summary: How much would a new Pajero cost if it were to come to the United States? Down Under has the clues.
whatHappening: Mitsubishi has announced pricing for the new Pajero in Australia, offering potential clues about what the full-size SUV might cost if it were reintroduced to the U.S. market. The Australian pricing could serve as a benchmark for American consumers wondering about potential availability and costs.
whoInvolved: Mitsubishi Motors, the Japanese automaker that has manufactured and marketed the Pajero globally since 1981, is at the center of this story. The company previously sold the vehicle in North America under the Montero nameplate before discontinuing it in the U.S.
whyMatters: The U.S. SUV market remains highly competitive and lucrative, and any indication of a potential Pajero return—complete with pricing signals—could influence consumer expectations and competitor strategy. For American buyers interested in full-size SUVs, Australian pricing provides concrete data for speculation about domestic availability and affordability.
articleBody:
Mitsubishi has released pricing for the new generation Pajero in Australia, and industry observers are using those figures to extrapolate what the legendary SUV might command if it returned to the U.S. market. The move reflects renewed interest in the model after years of absence from North American showrooms, with the Australian pricing providing a tangible starting point for cost discussions.

The Mitsubishi Pajero is a full-size SUV that has been manufactured and marketed globally by Mitsubishi Motors since 1981. In North America, it was previously known as the Mitsubishi Montero, while the United Kingdom knew it as the Shogun. The vehicle built a substantial following across multiple continents, though Mitsubishi eventually withdrew it from the U.S. market, leaving a gap in the company's SUV lineup that enthusiasts have long hoped to see filled.

According to Car and Driver, the Australian pricing serves as a useful reference point for estimating potential U.S. costs. Automakers often adjust pricing by market, accounting for local taxes, tariffs, and demand dynamics, but regional pricing can reveal manufacturing costs and target margins that inform predictions about other markets. Australia's position as a right-hand-drive market with different regulatory requirements means direct conversion isn't straightforward, yet the figures still offer meaningful context.

The reintroduction of the Pajero to any major market would represent a significant strategic move for Mitsubishi. The full-size SUV segment remains popular among buyers seeking three-row seating, towing capacity, and rugged capability. If the company decides to bring the model back to North America, pricing will be critical—it must position competitively against established rivals while reflecting the vehicle's premium positioning and the cost of meeting U.S. emissions and safety standards.

For now, enthusiasts and industry watchers are parsing the Australian numbers to construct educated guesses about American pricing. Whether this signals an imminent U.S. return or remains a market-by-market decision remains unclear, but the release of concrete Australian figures has reignited speculation about the Pajero's future on American roads.

title: RivianOS 2 Update Makes the R1 Look and Feel More Like an R2
summary: R1 owners will benefit from many of the improvements made to the R2's infotainment interface.
whatHappening: Rivian has released a RivianOS 2 update that brings key infotainment improvements from the newer R2 model to the existing R1 lineup. R1 owners will now enjoy a more refined and modern interface similar to what buyers of the upcoming R2 will experience.
whoInvolved: Rivian Automotive, Inc., an American electric vehicle manufacturer founded in 2009, is rolling out the update across its product line. The company produces the R1T pickup truck and R1S SUV, both built on a modular skateboard platform, alongside its electric delivery van used by Amazon.
whyMatters: The update enhances the user experience for existing R1 owners without requiring hardware changes, improving customer satisfaction and competitive positioning. This strategy also helps Rivian maintain software consistency across its model lineup as the company ramps up production of the R2, its upcoming mass-market entry.
articleBody:
Rivian is bringing its latest infotainment technology to current owners through the RivianOS 2 update, which ports several interface and usability improvements from the R2 model to the R1 lineup. According to Car and Driver, R1 owners will benefit from many of the improvements made to the R2's infotainment interface, representing a significant software enhancement that reflects the company's commitment to supporting its existing customer base.

Rivian Automotive, founded in 2009, has positioned itself as a premium electric vehicle manufacturer. The company began deliveries of its R1T pickup truck in late 2021 and expanded to the R1S sport utility vehicle in 2023, both vehicles built on the company's proprietary skateboard platform architecture. The skateboard design allows Rivian to share core technology across multiple vehicle types while maintaining flexibility for future models. The company also produces the Rivian EDV, an electric delivery van sold exclusively to Amazon for its logistics operations.

The RivianOS 2 update addresses a common challenge in the automotive industry: keeping software experiences fresh and competitive across a manufacturer's entire portfolio. By porting R2 infotainment innovations to the older R1 platform, Rivian ensures that early adopters continue to receive meaningful improvements long after their initial purchase. This approach strengthens customer loyalty during a critical period when the company is scaling production and preparing to launch new models.

For Rivian, software updates have become increasingly important as the company works to differentiate its vehicles in a crowding electric vehicle market. The R1 models represent the company's current flagships, appealing to customers seeking premium performance and technology. The forthcoming R2, positioned as a more accessible entry point to the Rivian brand, will compete in a different market segment. By harmonizing the software experience across both generations, Rivian signals that ownership experience matters as much as hardware specifications.

The update also reflects the scalability of Rivian's skateboard platform architecture. Because the R1 and R2 share fundamental technological underpinnings, software improvements developed for one model can be adapted and deployed to others without requiring extensive rework. This modular approach to vehicle design extends beyond the consumer market; Rivian has already licensed aspects of its platform architecture for use by other companies, suggesting the long-term strategy involves becoming a technology supplier as well as a direct vehicle manufacturer.

title: $20K Hustlers: 1994 Budget Sports Coupes Compared
summary: Blistering performance costs less than one game’s play for Barry Bonds.
whatHappening: Car and Driver is testing 1994 budget sports coupes priced around $20,000, offering surprising performance and thrills at an entry-level price point. The publication compares how much speed and driving excitement consumers can access without spending a fortune.
whoInvolved: Car and Driver, a leading automotive journalism outlet, is conducting the comparison. The article benchmarks performance-oriented coupes available to mainstream buyers in 1994, a year when such affordable sports cars were still viable market offerings.
whyMatters: This comparison illustrates how accessible high-performance driving was to average consumers in the mid-1990s, before sports car prices climbed significantly. The $20,000 price point—framed against Barry Bonds's single-game salary—underscores the relative affordability of genuine driving performance in that era.
articleBody:
The early 1990s represented a golden age for affordable sports cars, and Car and Driver's latest test proves the point by gathering a collection of 1994 budget coupes that deliver blistering performance for less than $20,000. According to Car and Driver, drivers shopping in this price range can find genuine thrills and track-ready engineering without the premium price tags that would dominate the sports car market just a decade later.

To put the value proposition in perspective, $20,000 in 1994 was less than a single game's earnings for Barry Bonds, the legendary left fielder who was then entering his second season with the San Francisco Giants after his 1986 debut with the Pittsburgh Pirates. Bonds would go on to become one of the greatest baseball players of all time, and his career earnings underscore just how affordable these performance machines were for the average enthusiast.

The vehicles tested represent a range of manufacturers' efforts to capture the budget-conscious performance market. Each contender was selected for its combination of accessible pricing, engaging driving dynamics, and genuine performance credentials. The coupes deliver the kind of acceleration and handling characteristics that would have previously required stepping up to more expensive segments.

This era of affordable sports car manufacturing reflects an industrial moment that would not last. By the early 2000s, cost pressures, regulatory requirements, and shifting market dynamics would push even entry-level performance vehicles into higher price brackets. The 1994 model year thus stands as a testament to an era when manufacturers still competed aggressively for the enthusiast buyer's limited budget.

For readers considering classic car investments or simply curious about automotive value history, the comparison serves as a reminder that genuine performance and engineering prowess were once attainable on an accessible budget. The test demonstrates what $20,000 could deliver when performance priorities aligned with production realities and manufacturer commitment to the grassroots sports car segment.

title: This BMW Roadster on Bring a Trailer Is Not What It Appears to Be
summary: It’s the perfect car for those with Z8 tastes but a Z4 budget.
whatHappening: A BMW roadster listed on Bring a Trailer is generating buzz for being a cleverly disguised alternative to more expensive models. The listing highlights a vehicle that captures the aesthetic and spirit of a premium BMW roadster at a significantly lower price point.
whoInvolved: Car and Driver is covering the listing, which appears on Bring a Trailer, the popular online auction platform for enthusiast vehicles. BMW, the German automaker, manufactured both the aspirational Z8 model (produced 1998–2003) and the more accessible Z4 line that the featured car apparently emulates or represents.
whyMatters: This story appeals to budget-conscious enthusiasts who admire high-end BMW roadster design but cannot justify the cost of premium models. It highlights how the used and modified car market enables buyers to access the styling and character of luxury vehicles through alternative routes, a trend that shapes pricing and desirability across the classic and contemporary roadster segment.
articleBody:
A BMW roadster currently listed on Bring a Trailer has caught the attention of enthusiasts for being far more than a straightforward purchase—it represents an ingenious solution for those who dream of Z8 ownership but operate with Z4 budgets. According to Car and Driver, the vehicle is a masterclass in delivering premium roadster appeal without the corresponding price tag.

The BMW Z8, produced by the German manufacturer from 1998 to 2003, remains one of the marque's most coveted roadsters. Developed under the codename "E52" between 1993 and 1999, the Z8 resulted from a design collaboration led by Chris Bangle, with Henrik Fisker handling the exterior design and Scott Lempert developing the interior. Its exclusivity and performance heritage have made Z8 examples highly sought after and expensive on the collector market.

In contrast, BMW's Z-series lineup—where "Z" stands for Zukunft, the German word for future—has produced multiple generations of roadsters at varying price points. The Z4, which represents the more accessible end of the Z roadster spectrum, offers genuine BMW roadster credentials but typically commands lower values than its Z8 cousin. This pricing gap has created an opportunity for creative buyers and builders.

The Bring a Trailer listing appears to bridge this divide, presenting a vehicle that delivers the visual drama and driving character buyers associate with the Z8 experience while remaining financially attainable. Whether through careful specification, restoration, or modification, the car demonstrates how the secondary market and enthusiast community continue to find innovative ways to make premium automotive experiences accessible to a broader audience.

For collectors and enthusiasts, such listings underscore the enduring appeal of BMW's roadster lineage and the ingenuity of those who navigate the gap between aspiration and budget. The listing invites buyers to consider what truly defines the roadster experience—and whether achieving it necessarily requires the premium price of the most celebrated models.

title: EV, Hybrid, or Gas Car: What’s Best for a Road Trip?
summary: We take a Honda Accord Hybrid, a Tesla Model 3, and a Volkswagen Jetta on a 750-plus-mile journey to find out.
whatHappening: Car and Driver is putting three popular vehicle powertrains head-to-head on a real-world 750-plus-mile road trip: a Honda Accord Hybrid, a Tesla Model 3, and a Volkswagen Jetta. The test aims to determine which drivetrain delivers the best practical experience for long-distance driving.
whoInvolved: Car and Driver, a major automotive publication, is conducting the test. The vehicles represent three major automakers: Honda (the Accord, a best-selling sedan since 1989 with over 19 million units sold worldwide), Tesla (the Model 3, introduced in 2017 as an affordable electric option that was the world's top-selling plug-in electric car from 2018 to 2020), and Volkswagen.
whyMatters: As electric vehicle adoption accelerates and consumers weigh powertrain options for long trips, real-world comparisons of charging time, range, fuel costs, and driver comfort become increasingly critical to purchasing decisions. This test provides practical data to help buyers understand whether EVs, hybrids, or traditional gas vehicles best suit their road-trip needs, directly influencing a significant market segment's car-buying choices.
articleBody:
As electric vehicles become more commonplace on American roads, prospective buyers face a growing decision: which powertrain truly works best for extended road trips? According to Car and Driver, the answer isn't obvious, which is why the publication took three fundamentally different vehicles on a 750-plus-mile journey to find out.

The test vehicles represent the three major powertrains available today. The Honda Accord Hybrid combines traditional combustion with electric motors, offering fuel efficiency without the charging infrastructure concerns of pure electric vehicles. The Tesla Model 3 represents the fully electric option—a battery electric powered mid-size sedan introduced in 2017 that was marketed as Tesla's more affordable entry point compared to the Model S and Model X. The Volkswagen Jetta provides the baseline: a conventional gas-powered sedan representing traditional automotive technology.

The Honda Accord itself carries significant weight in the American automotive landscape. Since becoming a four-door sedan in 1976, the model has been one of the best-selling cars in the United States since 1989. Worldwide, over 19 million units have been sold, making it one of the best-selling automobiles of all time. This pedigree means the hybrid variant inherits proven reliability and refinement, though hybridization adds complexity and cost to the established formula.

The Tesla Model 3's credentials are equally notable. From 2018 to 2020, it held the title of world's top-selling plug-in electric car before the Tesla Model Y crossover took over the spot. The Model 3's three-year reign demonstrates substantial consumer acceptance of long-range electric sedans, even as charging infrastructure and battery technology continue to evolve. On a long trip, however, the Model 3's dependence on charging networks and charging time presents a fundamentally different experience than refueling a gas or hybrid vehicle.

What matters most on a road trip—range, refueling time, cost per mile, comfort, and convenience—varies by vehicle type. A hybrid's ability to use either fuel or electricity potentially offers flexibility, while an electric vehicle's zero tailpipe emissions and low operating costs must be weighed against charging stops. A gas vehicle's established refueling infrastructure and quick fill-ups provide familiarity, but at potentially higher per-mile fuel costs. The real-world test translates these theoretical tradeoffs into concrete data that prospective buyers can use to evaluate their own travel patterns and priorities.

title: View Photos of the 1994 Budget Sports Coupes Comparison Test
summary: See the interior and exterior of the 1994 Nissan 240SX SE, Toyota Celica GT, Mitsubishi Eclipse GS-T, Ford Probe GT, Honda Prelude VTEC, Eagle Talon TSi AWD, Acura Integra GS-R from every angle.
whatHappening: Car and Driver has published a photo gallery showcasing seven sports coupes from the 1994 model year, offering detailed interior and exterior views of each vehicle from multiple angles. The comparison captures a pivotal moment in the affordable performance car segment, featuring competitors from Japan's major automakers plus offerings from Ford, Eagle, and Acura.
whoInvolved: Car and Driver, a leading automotive publication, assembled images of seven manufacturers' entries into the budget sports coupe category: Nissan, Toyota, Mitsubishi, Ford, Honda, Eagle, and Acura. These brands were competing intensely in the early 1990s to dominate the affordable performance market that appealed to younger buyers and enthusiasts.
whyMatters: This photo essay documents a distinctive era in automotive design when Japanese manufacturers and American competitors were locked in a fierce battle for the youth-oriented sports car market. The 1994 model year represented the peak of this segment's popularity before market consolidation and changing consumer preferences would reshape the category in subsequent decades.
articleBody:
Car and Driver has compiled a comprehensive photo gallery documenting the 1994 budget sports coupes comparison test, presenting the Nissan 240SX SE, Toyota Celica GT, Mitsubishi Eclipse GS-T, Ford Probe GT, Honda Prelude VTEC, Eagle Talon TSi AWD, and Acura Integra GS-R from every conceivable angle. The gallery captures both interior cabins and exterior styling of each vehicle, offering viewers a detailed visual record of how manufacturers approached the affordable performance segment during this pivotal year.

The Nissan 240SX, which entered the North American market in 1989 as a replacement for the 200SX, was reaching the end of its first generation during 1994. The S13 generation (1989–1994) was based on the Nissan S platform and represented a significant entry point for performance-minded drivers seeking rear-wheel-drive dynamics at an attainable price. By 1994, the redesigned S14 generation was preparing to launch, making the final year of the first-generation model an important snapshot of where Nissan's strategy stood in the market.

Toyota's Celica brought different positioning to the comparison. As a nameplate with roots extending back to 1970, the Celica had established itself as a sophisticated, design-focused alternative in the sports coupe space. The Celica name itself derives from the Latin word coelica, meaning heavenly or celestial, reflecting Toyota's premium positioning for the model. By the 1994 model year, the Celica had evolved through multiple generations and body styles, including convertibles, liftbacks, and notchback coupés, though the GT variant featured in this test represented the more performance-oriented direction.

According to Car and Driver's photographic documentation, the comparison also included Mitsubishi's Eclipse with turbo capability, Ford's Probe GT, Honda's Prelude equipped with VTEC variable valve timing technology, Eagle's Talon TSi in all-wheel-drive configuration, and Acura's Integra GS-R. Each vehicle represented distinct engineering philosophies and market strategies—from turbocharged power and all-wheel-drive systems to naturally aspirated high-revving engines and lightweight chassis designs.

The 1994 model year proved to be a watershed moment for this segment. The competition among these seven vehicles illustrated how thoroughly Japanese manufacturers had captured the imagination of performance enthusiasts with affordable, nimble automobiles, while American manufacturers struggled to maintain relevance in a category they had largely ceded. The detailed photographic comparison preserved a record of industrial design and engineering approaches that would soon become increasingly rare as market consolidation, rising safety and emissions standards, and shifting consumer preferences toward SUVs would systematically eliminate most of these models by the early 2000s.

This gallery serves as both a nostalgic document and a technical reference, allowing contemporary viewers to study the proportions, details, and design language that defined accessible performance cars at the moment before the category's gradual decline.

title: Say ‘I Do’ to This Wild British Wedding Car on BaT
summary: The 1996 Imperial Landaulette is based on an Austin taxi and powered by a Nissan diesel engine.
whatHappening: A distinctive 1996 Imperial Landaulette—a wedding car built on an Austin taxi chassis and powered by a Nissan diesel engine—is being offered for sale on Bring a Trailer. The unusual vehicle combines British taxi heritage with unconventional powertrain engineering.
whoInvolved: Car and Driver is reporting on the listing. The vehicle itself represents a niche segment of British automotive coachbuilding, where specialist manufacturers have historically adapted commercial taxi platforms for luxury or ceremonial use.
whyMatters: The sale highlights the enduring appeal of quirky, purpose-built British vehicles in the collector car market. It demonstrates how vintage taxi platforms continue to find second lives as bespoke vehicles, preserving automotive craftsmanship and British engineering ingenuity for enthusiasts and collectors.
articleBody:
A 1996 Imperial Landaulette is making its way to auction on Bring a Trailer, offering collectors a rare glimpse into British coachbuilding creativity. According to Car and Driver, the vehicle pairs an Austin taxi platform with a Nissan diesel engine—an unusual combination that reflects both the constraints and innovations of specialist British automotive manufacturers.

The Imperial Landaulette's foundation traces back to Austin's taxi heritage. The Austin FX3, produced from 1948 to 1958, established the lineage of London taxicabs designed to comply with strict Metropolitan Police Conditions of Fitness. Built by Carbodies of Coventry on Austin chassis, the FX3 became synonymous with dignified, purpose-built British transportation. Though the Landaulette is a later creation, it carries forward that same ethos of engineering vehicles for specific ceremonial and commercial roles.

The addition of a Nissan diesel engine represents a pragmatic evolution. By the 1990s, diesel powerplants offered improved fuel economy and durability compared to aging petrol engines, making them an attractive retrofit option for extended vehicle lifecycles. This powertrain choice would have given the wedding car reliable, economical operation for frequent use at ceremonies and events—practical engineering dressed in formal attire.

The Landaulette body style itself speaks to British automotive tradition. The convertible roof configuration, typical of wedding and ceremonial vehicles, provides the visual drama expected at formal occasions while maintaining the structural integrity of the taxi platform beneath. This marriage of utility and ceremony reflects how British coachbuilders have long found creative ways to repurpose commercial vehicles for upmarket applications.

The sale on Bring a Trailer underscores persistent collector interest in vehicles that embody specific moments and purposes in automotive history. A wedding car tells the story of celebrations it has witnessed, while its engineering documents the practical solutions manufacturers employed to extend vehicle usefulness. The Imperial Landaulette, with its mix of heritage platform and period-appropriate modernization, offers that narrative alongside mechanical intrigue.

title: View Exterior Photos of the 2027 Ram 2500 HD Power Wagon
summary: See the exterior of the 2027 Ram 2500 HD Power Wagon from every angle.
whatHappening: Car and Driver has released exterior photos of the upcoming 2027 Ram 2500 HD Power Wagon, offering a comprehensive visual preview of the truck from multiple angles. The images showcase the latest iteration of Ram's off-road-focused heavy-duty pickup ahead of its official market debut.
whoInvolved: Ram Trucks, a division of Stellantis North America, is behind the 2027 Power Wagon. The Power Wagon nameplate, originally used by Dodge from 1945 to 1980, was revived in 2005 as a four-wheel drive variant of the Ram 2500 and continues today as a premium package offering on Ram's 3/4-ton lineup.
whyMatters: The Power Wagon represents a key segment in Ram's portfolio—the high-end, adventure-focused truck market—and visual previews help potential buyers evaluate design changes and features before official specifications are released. For Ram Trucks, maintaining strong demand in the luxury off-road truck category is crucial to the brand's overall sales performance and brand positioning.
articleBody:
The 2027 Ram 2500 HD Power Wagon has been revealed through exterior photography, giving enthusiasts and potential buyers an early look at the design direction for Ram's most rugged heavy-duty offering. According to Car and Driver, the images present the truck from every angle, providing comprehensive coverage of styling updates and visual refinements for the new model year.

The Power Wagon carries significant historical weight within Ram's lineup. Originally established as the legendary Dodge Power Wagon—a four-wheel drive medium-duty truck produced from 1945 to 1980—the nameplate was revived for the 2005 model year as a premium variant of the Dodge Ram 2500. When Ram became an independent brand following its 2009 spin-off from Dodge, the Power Wagon transitioned as well, establishing itself as a distinctive special package of the four-wheel drive version of Ram's 3/4-ton 2500 model.

Ram Trucks, operating as a division of Stellantis North America, has built its reputation on the slogan "Guts. Glory. Ram," and the Power Wagon embodies that philosophy with its off-road capabilities and rugged construction. The 2500 platform serves as the foundation for heavy-duty applications, and the Power Wagon variant layers on specialized features designed for serious trail work and extreme terrain navigation.

The exterior photography release marks a typical pre-launch strategy for major automotive introductions, allowing the brand to build anticipation and media coverage without revealing full technical specifications or pricing details. For a truck positioned at the premium end of the market, visual appeal and aggressive styling cues are critical marketing elements that influence buyer perception and purchase decisions.

The 2027 model year update represents Ram's continued investment in the Power Wagon segment, a niche but highly profitable category within the light to mid-weight pickup market. As the automotive industry navigates shifting consumer preferences and regulatory pressures, maintaining enthusiasm for capability-focused trucks remains a strategic priority for Stellantis and its Ram division.

title: VW Approves Plan to Reduce Lineup by 50 Percent and Cut 50,000 Jobs
summary: The automaker says it intends to reduce the complexity of its offerings by 75 percent, with fewer variants and stronger economies of scale.
whatHappening: Volkswagen has approved a sweeping restructuring plan that will shrink its product lineup by half and eliminate 50,000 jobs. The automaker aims to reduce the complexity of its offerings by 75 percent through fewer variants and improved economies of scale.
whoInvolved: Volkswagen, the German automobile brand and flagship of the Volkswagen Group conglomerate, is implementing the changes. The company, which has grown into a global brand over 81 years since its post-World War II revival and was the world's second-largest automaker by sales in 2024, is owned by Porsche SE and the Porsche-Piëch family.
whyMatters: The job cuts represent a significant workforce reduction that will reshape the automaker's operations and likely affect manufacturing communities across Europe and beyond. The streamlined product strategy signals VW's attempt to navigate competitive pressure and improve profitability through operational efficiency, though the scale of disruption underscores mounting challenges in the global automotive industry.
articleBody:
Volkswagen has greenlighted an ambitious restructuring effort that will fundamentally reshape the German automaker's business operations. According to Car and Driver, the company plans to reduce its vehicle lineup by 50 percent while eliminating 50,000 jobs as part of a broader efficiency drive. The initiative aims to cut the complexity of VW's product offerings by 75 percent, relying on fewer variants across its portfolio to achieve stronger economies of scale.

The move reflects Volkswagen's effort to streamline operations amid intensifying competition in the automotive sector. As the flagship brand of the Volkswagen Group—a multinational conglomerate headquartered in Wolfsburg, Lower Saxony—VW has built a global reputation over more than eight decades since its revival following World War II. The brand is particularly known for the iconic Beetle, but today markets a diverse range of vehicles across multiple segments and price points worldwide.

The job reductions will be substantial, affecting tens of thousands of employees across the company's operations. Such significant workforce cuts typically concentrate pain in manufacturing and related functions, with potential ripple effects through supply chains and regional economies where VW maintains major production facilities. The exact timing and geographic distribution of these layoffs remain key details for affected workers and communities.

By consolidating its model range and reducing product variants, Volkswagen aims to lower production costs and improve manufacturing efficiency. Fewer variants mean longer production runs of each model, better utilization of factory capacity, and simpler supply chain management. This strategy is designed to make the company more competitive while freeing resources for investment in areas like electric vehicle development and digital capabilities.

The restructuring also signals management's response to broader pressures reshaping the global auto industry. As the company—now valued at approximately $58.9 billion—navigates the transition to electrification and faces competition from both traditional automakers and new entrants, operational efficiency has become critical. VW's decision to prioritize scale and simplification over breadth suggests leadership believes the market can support fewer but stronger product offerings from the brand.

title: Leno's Law Is Now One Step Away from Final Approval
summary: A new provision helped the bill easily get through the California Senate, with the governor's signature the last step before it becomes law.
whatHappening: Leno's Law has cleared the California State Senate and is now awaiting the governor's signature to become official law. A new provision in the bill helped it pass easily through the upper chamber of the state legislature.
whoInvolved: The California State Senate, the upper house of the California State Legislature that convenes at the State Capitol in Sacramento, has voted to advance the measure. The Governor of California, who serves as head of government and commander-in-chief of state forces, will deliver the final approval needed.
whyMatters: The bill's passage through the Senate represents a major milestone after a new provision resolved key obstacles to its advancement. Once signed by the governor, Leno's Law will move from legislative approval into actual implementation, making it enforceable across California.
articleBody:
Leno's Law has successfully navigated a critical hurdle in the legislative process, clearing the California State Senate with ease following the addition of a new provision that addressed outstanding concerns. The bill now sits on the governor's desk awaiting signature—the final procedural step required to transform it from legislation into binding law.

whatHappening: Bristol Cars, the defunct British luxury automaker, is returning to production by completing five V-10 supercars that were left unfinished when the original company collapsed. whoInvolved: Bristol Cars Limited was a British manufacturer of hand-built luxury cars headquartered in Bristol, England, originally formed from the car division of the Bristol Aeroplane Company after World War II. The company entered liquidation in February 2020 after being placed in receivership and taken over in 2011, but is now being revived to complete its remaining inventory.
whyMatters: This revival represents a rare second act for a storied but struggling luxury carmaker, signaling renewed interest in completing heritage vehicles even after company collapse. For collectors and enthusiasts, it offers a chance to finally obtain the supercars they ordered, while demonstrating the enduring appeal of Bristol's exclusive, hand-crafted approach to automotive engineering.
articleBody:
Bristol Cars is making an unlikely return from the dead. The eccentric British marque, which has been dormant since entering liquidation in February 2020, is restarting production to complete five V-10 supercars that were left unfinished when the original company collapsed. According to Car and Driver, these vehicles represent a chance to fulfill orders placed years earlier, breathing new life into a storied but troubled manufacturer.

Bristol Cars was born from the car division of the Bristol Aeroplane Company in the years following World War II, eventually becoming independent as Bristol Cars Limited. The company built a reputation for hand-crafted luxury vehicles, each one assembled with meticulous attention to detail. Over its decades of operation, Bristol Cars cultivated a cult following among collectors who valued exclusivity and craftsmanship over mass-market appeal.

But the company's journey was marked by financial turbulence. After being placed in receivership and taken over in 2011, Bristol Cars struggled to maintain operations. The firm ultimately entered liquidation in February 2020, leaving a backlog of incomplete vehicles in its wake. Among these unfinished projects were five high-performance supercars equipped with V-10 engines—prestigious machines that customers had ordered but never received.

The decision to complete these five vehicles signals a return to production for the marque. Rather than starting from scratch with entirely new designs, the restart leverages existing inventory and customer commitments, reducing the capital and development risk associated with relaunch. For collectors who placed orders years ago, completion of these supercars represents the fulfillment of long-deferred expectations.

The revival also underscores the enduring appeal of Bristol's hand-built philosophy. In an industry dominated by mass production and automation, the company's bespoke approach continues to resonate with buyers willing to pay premium prices for vehicles assembled by craftspeople rather than robots. The V-10 supercars represent the pinnacle of that ethos—powerful, exclusive machines made in limited numbers.

title: From the Archive: 1995 Nissan Sentra GXE
summary: What they mean in 1995 by 'more car.'
whatHappening: Car and Driver revisits the 1995 Nissan Sentra GXE, exploring what the automaker meant by delivering 'more car' in that model year. The piece examines the features and value proposition of this compact sedan from nearly three decades ago.
whoInvolved: Nissan, the Japanese multinational automobile manufacturer headquartered in Yokohama, manufactured the Sentra as part of its core lineup. The Sentra has been in production since 1982 and was positioned as an export version of the Japanese Nissan Sunny during this era.
whyMatters: Archival automotive retrospectives like this offer insight into how automakers marketed value and features in earlier decades, revealing shifting consumer expectations and industry standards. Understanding the 1995 Sentra's positioning helps contextualize how compact car segments have evolved and what 'more car for your money' meant before modern safety tech, infotainment systems, and efficiency standards reshaped the category.
articleBody:
The 1995 Nissan Sentra GXE represents a snapshot of automotive value from the mid-1990s, when Japanese compact cars were carving out a reputation for affordability and reliability. According to Car and Driver, the GXE trim embodied what Nissan considered 'more car'—a promise to deliver increased capability and comfort within the compact segment. At the time, this positioning reflected Nissan's broader strategy of offering accessible, feature-rich vehicles to cost-conscious American buyers.

The Sentra in 1995 occupied Nissan's subcompact class, a category it would retain until 1999 when it transitioned to the compact car classification. As an export version of the Japanese Nissan Sunny, the Sentra shared engineering and platform fundamentals with the domestic Japanese model, allowing Nissan to leverage economies of scale while tailoring features and trim levels for North American markets. The GXE trim sat in the middle of the Sentra lineup, balancing base-model simplicity with more upscale variants.

During this era, 'more car' for compact-sedan buyers typically meant practical advantages: adequate interior space, responsive handling, and dependable mechanical systems. The mid-1990s predated the integration of complex electronics, touchscreens, and advanced driver-assistance systems that define modern vehicles. Instead, value was communicated through straightforward metrics—engine performance, fuel economy, warranty coverage, and the quantity of standard amenities like power windows, air conditioning, and sound systems.

Nissan's compact cars had established strong footholds in the American market by the 1990s, building on decades of export success that traced back to the company's origins in the early 20th century. The Sentra line benefited from this reputation, attracting buyers seeking alternatives to American domestic compact offerings. The GXE trim specifically targeted buyers willing to spend modestly more than base-model prices in exchange for enhanced comfort and convenience.

Archival features like this one illuminate how automotive value propositions have shifted. The technological, safety, and efficiency standards that buyers now expect as standard were either unavailable or positioned as luxury features in 1995. Examining what the 1995 Sentra GXE offered reveals not just the capabilities of that vehicle, but the baseline expectations and aspirations of car buyers in that decade—a useful historical marker for understanding how the compact car segment has transformed.

articleBody:

title: I See Dead Cars: A Mailman's Daily Trip Down Memory Lane
summary: "Men are tormented with the opinions they have of things, not by the things themselves." —Epictetus
whatHappening: A mailman is sharing observations about abandoned and deteriorating vehicles he encounters on his daily postal route. His reflections use classical philosophy to frame how our perceptions shape our experiences with these forgotten cars.
whoInvolved: A postal carrier whose routine work brings him into contact with decaying automobiles in neighborhoods across his delivery area. Car and Driver, the automotive publication, is covering this mailman's philosophical perspective on vehicles left to rot.
whyMatters: The story captures how ordinary workers witness urban decay and automotive waste in ways that mainstream culture often overlooks. It bridges practical, everyday observation with philosophical inquiry, suggesting that how we perceive neglected things—whether cars or broader societal decline—reflects our own mindsets rather than objective reality.
articleBody:
A mail carrier's daily rounds have become an unintended catalog of automotive mortality. Each street he walks reveals cars in various states of abandonment: rusted frames, flat tires, windshields clouded with grime, vehicles that have not moved in months or years. According to Car and Driver, this mailman has begun reflecting on what these dead cars represent and what they say about the neighborhoods and the people who leave them behind.

His observations are framed through an unexpected lens: the ancient Stoic philosophy of Epictetus. The first-century Greek philosopher, who spent much of his life in Rome before his banishment to Nicopolis in northwestern Greece, left behind a striking assertion about human suffering and perception. "Men are tormented with the opinions they have of things, not by the things themselves," Epictetus wrote. The mailman has adopted this framework to understand his daily encounters with derelict vehicles. The cars themselves are simply metal and rust; the torment comes from the stories we construct around them and the decline they symbolize.

This philosophical angle proves surprisingly apt for examining urban landscapes where abandoned cars accumulate. A vehicle left to decay on a residential street tells a story—of financial hardship, of broken dreams, of neighborhoods that no longer attract investment or care. But the mailman's application of Epictetus suggests that our distress at seeing such decay is not caused by the rusted metal itself but by the narrative we overlay on it. We torment ourselves with interpretations: decline, abandonment, loss.

What makes this observation particularly resonant is how it challenges viewers to examine their own relationship with decay. The mailman encounters these cars not as a mechanic analyzing mechanical failure, nor as a real estate appraiser measuring neighborhood depreciation, but simply as a person who passes them every working day. His position gives him an unusual vantage point—consistent, repeated, unglamorous exposure to the material consequences of economic and personal misfortune.

The broader implications touch on how we process urban decline and environmental decay. If our suffering comes not from the things themselves but from our opinions of them, then perhaps the antidote is not only material restoration—cleaning up the streets, removing abandoned vehicles—but also a shift in how we interpret what we see. This does not dismiss the real problems these abandoned cars represent. Rather, it suggests that even while we work to address the underlying causes of automotive and urban decay, we might benefit from examining the stories we tell ourselves about what these objects mean.

title: The 2027 Supersports Is Bentley’s First Real Track Star
summary: An extensive training regimen transforms Bentley’s luxury coupe into a toned athlete.
whatHappening: Bentley is launching the 2027 Supersports, a track-focused variant of its luxury coupe designed to deliver genuine performance capabilities. The model represents the brand's first serious attempt at creating a vehicle optimized for the race circuit rather than the road.

whyMatters: The Supersports signals Bentley's strategic pivot toward performance authenticity, blending its traditional luxury positioning with genuine track capability. This move could redefine how ultra-premium manufacturers approach the intersection of exclusivity and motorsport credibility.
articleBody:
Bentley has announced the 2027 Supersports, marking a significant departure from the brand's traditional focus on grand touring luxury. Rather than simply adding aesthetic enhancements or minor performance tweaks, the new model undergoes what the automaker describes as an extensive training regimen—a comprehensive program of engineering refinement designed to transform the luxury coupe into a genuine track athlete.

The British manufacturer, founded by W. O. Bentley in 1919, has long carried the prestige of motorsport success. The company's racing pedigree is unmatched in the luxury segment, with victories at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1924, 1927, 1928, 1929, 1930, and again in 2003. Yet in recent decades, Bentley has largely positioned itself as a purveyor of refined comfort and opulence rather than visceral performance. The 2027 Supersports represents an intentional effort to reconnect with that competitive DNA.

According to Car and Driver, the development approach mirrors athletic conditioning—the vehicle undergoes systematic optimization across multiple systems and components to achieve track performance. This suggests modifications extend beyond engine tuning to encompass suspension geometry, aerodynamic refinement, braking systems, and weight reduction strategies. For a brand owned by the Volkswagen Group since 1998 and consolidated under Audi's premium operations since 2022, this level of performance focus represents a strategic statement about where Bentley sees its future.

The significance of this move lies not merely in horsepower figures or lap times, but in what it signals about luxury automotive identity. The Supersports challenges the assumption that exclusivity and affordability must come at the expense of authentic capability. By investing in genuine track engineering rather than cosmetic sportiness, Bentley is betting that discerning customers—particularly those with experience on circuits—value real performance credentials over merely aggressive styling.

The 2027 Supersports also carries historical resonance. A century after Bentley's founding, the marque is returning to racing-inspired principles at a moment when the entire automotive industry faces pressure to prove relevance beyond traditional metrics. Whether through electrification strategies or track-focused variants, manufacturers must demonstrate they can evolve without abandoning their core identity. For Bentley, this means proving that luxury and performance need not be opposing forces.

title: Who Teaches a Robotaxi’s Remote Helpers? SAE Has a Driver’s Ed Plan
summary: Operators of Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous vehicles require a particular set of skills.
whatHappening: SAE International is developing a formal training and certification program for remote operators who control Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous vehicles. The initiative addresses a growing need to standardize skills and qualifications for workers managing robotaxis and other driverless fleets from remote locations.
whoInvolved: SAE International, a global professional association and standards organization based in Warrendale, Pennsylvania, is spearheading the effort. The organization, which expanded beyond its original automotive engineering focus to include aerospace and autonomous vehicle standards, is positioning itself as the authority for operator certification.
whyMatters: As autonomous vehicle fleets scale up, standardizing operator training becomes critical for safety, liability, and workforce development. Remote operation of robotaxis represents an entirely new job category, and establishing clear educational pathways could shape how the autonomous vehicle industry manages human oversight and emergency response.
articleBody:
SAE International is creating a structured training and certification program for remote operators of autonomous vehicles, marking a significant step toward professionalizing a workforce that barely existed a few years ago. The initiative, according to Car and Driver, reflects the urgent need to establish consistent standards as Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous vehicle deployments expand beyond pilot programs into commercial operations at scale.

Remote operators of robotaxis and autonomous fleets perform a specialized function that differs fundamentally from traditional driving. Rather than controlling the vehicle moment-to-moment, these workers monitor operations from a distance and intervene when needed—responding to technical failures, assisting with edge cases the vehicle's artificial intelligence cannot resolve, or taking control during unexpected situations. The job demands a hybrid skill set that blends traditional automotive knowledge with technology proficiency and situational judgment.

SAE International, which evolved from the Society of Automotive Engineers to encompass a broader scope including aerospace and commercial autonomous vehicles, has the technical credibility and industry reach to establish such standards. The organization's involvement signals that remote operator training is being treated as a professional discipline rather than an ad hoc onboarding process individual companies devise internally. Standardization across the industry could improve safety consistency and worker mobility, allowing certified operators to transition between employers more easily.

The timing of this initiative reflects market realities. Companies deploying robotaxis at scale—from Waymo to emerging autonomous vehicle startups—are already hiring remote operators, but without agreed-upon training frameworks, each organization trains workers differently. A formal curriculum would establish baseline competencies, define escalation procedures, and create measurable performance metrics across the industry.

Developing curriculum for remote vehicle operation presents unique pedagogical challenges. Traditional driver's education focuses on vehicle control and road rules; remote operator training must emphasize system monitoring, decision-making under ambiguity, and crisis management in real time. SAE's program will likely combine classroom instruction on autonomous vehicle architecture, simulation-based practice scenarios, and supervised operational experience.

As autonomous vehicles transition from experimental technology to commercial infrastructure, the workers enabling that transition deserve formal recognition and pathways for advancement. SAE's driver's education plan for remote operators acknowledges that professionalism and standardization will be essential to public trust and operational reliability.

title: 'Days of Thunder' Sequel Will Hit Theaters in Summer 2028
summary: Tom Cruise reprises his role from the 1990 NASCAR movie and is joined by Anne Hathaway and director Jonathan Levine.
whatHappening: A sequel to the 1990 NASCAR action film Days of Thunder is in development and will arrive in theaters in Summer 2028. Tom Cruise is returning to his iconic role, joined by Anne Hathaway and director Jonathan Levine.
whoInvolved: Tom Cruise, one of Hollywood's most bankable stars whose films have grossed over $13.3 billion worldwide, will reprise his lead role. Anne Hathaway joins the cast, and Jonathan Levine will direct the project. The original 1990 film was directed by Tony Scott and featured Cruise alongside Robert Duvall, Nicole Kidman, and real-life NASCAR racers.
whyMatters: The sequel represents a major studio bet on legacy IP and reflects Hollywood's continued reliance on established franchises with proven box-office appeal. With Cruise's star power and a Summer 2028 release date, the film aims to capture both nostalgic audiences and new viewers interested in high-octane racing drama. The project also signals confidence in the action-thriller genre's commercial viability in the coming years.
articleBody:
Hollywood is revving up for a return to the racetrack. Tom Cruise will reprise his role from the 1990 NASCAR action drama Days of Thunder in a sequel set to hit theaters in Summer 2028, according to Car and Driver. The project will also star Anne Hathaway and be directed by Jonathan Levine, marking a significant studio commitment to bringing back a beloved 1990s franchise.

The original Days of Thunder, directed by Tony Scott and produced by Don Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer, was a star-studded vehicle that paired Cruise with Robert Duvall, Nicole Kidman, Randy Quaid, and Michael Rooker. The screenplay was written by Robert Towne based on a story he co-wrote with Cruise himself, and the film featured appearances by real-life NASCAR racers including Richard Petty, Rusty Wallace, Neil Bonnett, and Harry Gant. It became a defining sports action film of its era, blending high-speed racing sequences with interpersonal drama.

Cruse's involvement in the sequel underscores his status as one of Hollywood's most bankable stars. As of 2026, his films have grossed more than $13.3 billion worldwide, making him among the highest-grossing actors of all time. Throughout his career, he has earned an Honorary Palme d'Or, an Academy Honorary Award, and three Golden Globes, along with four competitive Academy Award nominations. His willingness to return to Days of Thunder signals strong confidence in the property's revival potential.

The addition of Anne Hathaway to the cast brings another A-list name to the project, though her specific role remains undisclosed. Jonathan Levine, tapped to direct, takes over the helm from Tony Scott, who helmed the original. The shift in creative leadership suggests the filmmakers aim to contemporize the franchise while honoring its high-octane roots.

The Summer 2028 release date positions the sequel within a competitive blockbuster season, indicating studio expectations for wide theatrical appeal. The revival of Days of Thunder reflects Hollywood's ongoing strategy of leveraging established intellectual property and star power to anchor major releases, particularly in the action and sports drama genres.
